2.x: Oxygen is the most abundant element by weight in the crust, followed by silicon at about 27.72%.
xa: **Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal**; **iron** second.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates (iron-rich core).

2.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust by weight?
2.x: Aluminium (about 8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust, followed by iron (about 5%) and calcium (about 3.6%). Silicon (about 27.7%) is more abundant but is not a metal; oxygen is the most abundant element overall.
2.tq: Element order O > Si > Al > Fe; most abundant metal = Al.
xs: **Aluminium** (**8.13%**) is the most abundant **metal** in the crust — option **(2)**.
**Iron** (**5.00%**) is second; **calcium** (**3.63%**) next.
**Silicon** (**27.72%**) is more abundant but not a metal.
xa: **Oxygen** (**46.60%**) is the most abundant element overall.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates.

2.s: Which of the following statements about the composition of Earth’s crust is incorrect?
o: Aluminium constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third.
Silicon constitutes 27.72% by weight and ranks second.
Iron constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third.
Oxygen constitutes 46.60% by weight and ranks first.
2.x: Option C is incorrect: iron is about 5% and ranks fourth. Aluminium is third at 8.13%, after oxygen (46.60%) and silicon (27.72%).
2.tq: Check the rank and figure of each element.
n: Oxygen constitutes 46.60% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Oxygen ranks first among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Silicon constitutes 27.72% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Silicon ranks second among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Aluminium constitutes 8.13% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Aluminium ranks third among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Iron constitutes 5.00% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Iron ranks fourth among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**Iron constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third**" — option **(3)**: iron is **5.00%** and ranks **fourth**.
**8.13%** and **third rank** belong to **aluminium**.
The others are correct: **oxygen 46.60%** (first), **silicon 27.72%** (second).
xa: Then **calcium 3.63%**, **sodium 2.83%**, **potassium 2.59%**, **magnesium 2.09%**.
**Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal** in the crust; **iron** second.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
**Whole Earth:** **iron** dominates (core is iron-rich).

2.s: What is SIMA mainly composed of?
2.x: SIMA stands for silica and magnesium (basalt); SIAL is silica and aluminium, NIFE nickel and iron.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
2.x: NIFE (nickel and iron) forms the core. SIAL is granitic and forms continents; SIMA is basaltic.
2.tq: match

2.s: Oxygen makes up about what percentage of the Earth's crust by weight?
2.x: Oxygen, at 46.60%, is the most abundant element of the crust; silicon is 27.72%, aluminium 8.13% and iron 5%.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: What does the term ‘NIFE’ refer to?
2.x: NIFE stands for nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe, ferrum), the main metals of Earth's core. N and F would wrongly suggest nitrogen and fluorine.
2.tq: Read the chemical symbols in the acronym.
n: NIFE means nickel and ferrum, or iron. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xs: **NIFE** stands for **Nickel and Ferrum (iron)** — option **(3)**.
The term comes from **E. Suess**, whose chemical zones were **SIAL**, **SIMA** and **NIFE**; NIFE is the **core** (BPSC **2022**).
The other options wrongly read "N" as **nitrogen** or "F" as **fluorine**.
xa: **Iron** is the core's **main constituent**; **nickel** is **another major constituent**.
**SIAL** = silica + aluminium (granite, continents); **SIMA** = silica + magnesium (basalt, source of magma).
NIFE density ~**11**; it explains Earth's **magnetism**.
Lighter elements in the core: **silicon** (APPSC G2 **2017** answer), sulphur, oxygen.

2.s: Which of the following lighter elements is found in the Earth's core besides iron and nickel?
2.x: Besides iron and nickel, the core holds lighter elements such as silicon, sulphur and oxygen, not aluminium, sodium or potassium.

2.s:
Consider the following statements about the Earth's core:
1. It is made mainly of iron and nickel.
2. Aluminium is one of its important lighter elements.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
2.x: The core is mainly iron and nickel; its lighter elements are silicon, sulphur and oxygen, not aluminium.

2.s: Who gave the terms SIAL, SIMA and NIFE for the layers of the Earth?
2.x: SIAL, SIMA and NIFE are the terms of Suess for the layers by their main elements.

2.s: What will happen if a conducting coil of wire is moved through a magnetic field?
2.src: APPSC Lecturers in Govt Degree Colleges Paper-I General Stud
2.x: Moving a coil through a magnetic field induces a current (Faraday's electromagnetic induction).

2.s: The upper mantle of earth is made mostly of
2.src: Technical Assistant (Geophysics), Technical Assistants in AP
2.x: The upper mantle is made mostly of silicate minerals (rich in iron and magnesium); molten iron and nickel belong to the outer core.

2.s: This is the largest of all the layers of planet Earth.
2.x: The mantle is the largest layer – about 83% of the Earth's volume and 68% of its mass.

2.s: In the structure of planet Earth, below the mantle, the core is mainly made up of which one of the following?
2.x: The core below the mantle is made mainly of iron (with nickel – NIFE).

2.s: In the structure of planet Earth, below the mantle, the core is mainly made up of which one of the following ?
2.x: The core is mainly iron with nickel; aluminium, chromium and silicon are not its main constituents.

2.s: The Earth’s magnetic field is due to :
o: Presence of a huge magnet at is centre
2.x: The geomagnetic field comes from electric currents in the conducting liquid outer core (geodynamo), not from a giant magnet at the centre.

2.s: The magnetic axis of the Earth is inclined by approximately how much to its geographic axis?
2.x: The Earth's magnetic axis is inclined approximately 11.5° to its geographic axis.
2.tq: Distinguish magnetic-axis inclination from the better-known seasonal axial tilt.
xs: The magnetic axis is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis — option **(2)**.
The field is made by **convecting molten iron** in the **outer core** (geodynamo).
xa: Iron accounts for Earth's **magnetism and rigidity**.
Swarm (**ESA**): outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from **westward** to **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.
Magnetic reversals last up to **~70,000 years**.

2.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the general variation of temperature, pressure and density inside the Earth?
o: Temperature increases, but pressure and density decrease with depth.
Temperature, pressure and density generally increase with depth.
2.x: Temperature, pressure and density all generally rise with increasing depth inside the Earth.
2.tq: Identify the common direction of the three internal gradients.
xs: **Temperature, pressure and density all rise with depth** — option **(2)**.
Pressure rises with the **weight of overlying rock**.
Density goes **2.8-3.0 (crust) → 4.6 (mantle) → 11-13.6 (core)**.
xa: Temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** in the upper crust; the rate slows deeper.
Pressure keeps the **inner core solid**.
India's geothermal wells must reach **2-5 km**.

2.s: What is the approximate geothermal gradient in the upper crust?
2.x: Temperature rises by approximately 1°C for every 32 m of depth in the upper crust, although the rate slows at greater depths.
2.tq: Pay attention to the place value in the depth-temperature relationship.
xs: In the upper crust temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** — option **(1)**.
The rate **slows deeper**.
xa: **Temperature, pressure and density** all rise with depth.
Highest geothermal potential: **Puga Valley** (**Ladakh**).
Other sites: **Manikaran** (HP), **Tattapani** (Chhattisgarh), **Cambay** (Gujarat), **Bakreshwar** (WB).

2.s: Why is the magnetic field generated by the Earth's liquid outer core important for life?
o: Shields life from solar wind and cosmic radiation
2.x: The magnetic field generated by the liquid outer core helps shield life from the solar wind and cosmic radiation.
xa: The magnetic axis is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis.
Magnetic **reversals** can last up to **~70,000 years**.
**Swarm (ESA)**: outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from sluggish **westward** to strong **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.

2.s: In which State is the Bakreshwar geothermal site located?
2.x: Bakreshwar is in West Bengal; Cambay is the geothermal site of Gujarat, Manikaran of Himachal Pradesh and Tattapani of Chhattisgarh.

2.s: In which layer does convection of conducting material generate the Earth's magnetic field?
2.x: Convection in the liquid outer core generates the field, and changes in that flow are linked to field reversals.
n: Movement and convection of conducting material in the liquid outer core produce the geodynamo. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The geodynamo generates Earth’s magnetic field. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Magnetic-field reversals are linked to changes in molten-core movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: The **magnetic axis** is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis.
**Swarm (ESA):** outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from **westward** to **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.
Magnetic reversals have lasted up to ~**70,000 years**.

2.s: What is the approximate average density of the Earth?
2.x: Earth averages about 5.5 g/cm³, the densest planet, with density increasing inward.
n: Earth’s average density is approximately 5.5 g/cm³. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Earth is the densest planet. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Earth’s density generally increases inward. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Heavier materials are concentrated in Earth’s core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Density gradient: **2.8–3.0** (crust) → **4.6** (mantle) → **11–13.6** (core).
**Temperature, pressure and density** all **rise with depth**.
Temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** in the upper crust.

2.s: Through which of the following do diamonds mainly reach the Earth's crust from the mantle?
2.x: Diamonds formed in the mantle are transported upward to the crust through kimberlite pipes.
2.tq: Match the resource with its geological transport pathway.
xs: Diamonds reach the crust through **kimberlite pipes** — option **(1)**.
They **form in the mantle**.
xa: **Madhya Pradesh** has **~90%** of India's reserves.
Mantle: Moho to **2,900 km**, silicates rich in **iron and magnesium**.
Mantle: **83%** of volume.

2.s: Which State is associated with approximately 90% of India's diamond reserves?
2.x: Madhya Pradesh is associated with approximately 90% of India's diamond reserves.
2.tq: Link the percentage resource fact with the correct State rather than a geothermal location.
xs: **Madhya Pradesh** has **~90%** of India's diamond reserves — option **(2)**.
Diamonds form in the **mantle** and reach the crust via **kimberlite pipes**.
xa: **Puga Valley** (Ladakh) has the highest **geothermal** potential.
**Bakreshwar** (WB) and **Cambay** (Gujarat) are geothermal sites.
The liquid outer core's field shields life from **solar wind**.

2.s: Where is the Puga Valley geothermal field located?
2.x: Puga Valley in Ladakh is India's highest geothermal field.

2.s: Which ESA mission found that the outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from westward to eastward?
2.x: ESA's Swarm satellites showed the outer-core flow under the Pacific switched direction, weakening around 2020.

2.s:
Match the following:
List-I (Geothermal site)
A. Manikaran
B. Tattapani
C. Cambay
D. Bakreshwar
List-II (State)
1. Gujarat
2. West Bengal
3. Himachal Pradesh

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
2.x: Manikaran is in Himachal Pradesh, Tattapani in Chhattisgarh, Cambay in Gujarat and Bakreshwar in West Bengal.

2.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Iron is the main constituent of the core.
Nickel is another major constituent of the core.
2.x: Option B is incorrect: the outer core is liquid, which is why S-waves stop there. The inner core is solid and the core is mainly iron and nickel.
2.tq: Discriminate the state of each layer.
n: The outer core is liquid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The inner core is solid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The main constituent of the core is iron. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Nickel is another major constituent of the core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**The outer core is solid**" — option **(2)**: the outer core is **liquid**, so **S-waves stop** there.
The other statements are correct: **iron** is the **main constituent**, **nickel** another major one, and the **inner core is solid**.
xa: The inner core is called the **NIFE** or **solid core**; density **13.3–13.6**.
**Pressure** keeps the inner core solid despite the heat.
⚠ Outer core **liquid**, inner core **solid**.
The core begins at about **2,900 km** depth.

2.s: What is personality?
o: The outer appearance of the individuals
2.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II (Male & Female) in AP
2.x: The printed key (personality = the behaviour of individuals, the sum of one's behaviour patterns) is kept; definitions such as Allport's stress inner psychophysical systems, so B is a tempting rival.

2.s: Gramsabha constitutes of:
2.src: APPSC Group-III Mains Panchayat Secretary (Grade-IV) Paper-I
2.at: All persons included in the electoral rolls
2.x: Under Art. 243A the Gram Sabha consists of all persons registered in the electoral rolls of the village within the panchayat area.

2.s: Photons are?
2.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-I General St
2.x: Photons are particles (quanta) of light.

2.s: Phonons are?
2.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-I General St
2.x: Phonons are quanta of vibration (sound) in solids – 'sound particles'; photons are light particles.

3.s: The second-most abundant metal in earth's crust is:
3.src: APPSC Divisional Accounts Officer (Mains) General Studies &
3.x: Aluminium (8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust and iron (5.0%) is the second.

3.s: In which of the following activities silicon carbide is used?
3.src: APPSC Junior Assistant cum Computer Assistant in ANGRAU Gene
3.x: Silicon carbide (carborundum) is extremely hard, so it is used as an abrasive for cutting and grinding very hard substances (it is also a power semiconductor).

3.s: The Integrated Chip (IC) of a computer is usually made of:
3.src: APPSC Forest Range Officers Mains General Studies & Mental A
3.x: Integrated circuits are made on silicon chips (a semiconductor). Off-topic (computers), moved.

3.s: Which is the second-most abundant element in the Earth's crust by weight?
3.x: Silicon ranks second at about 27.7%; iron is the second-most abundant metal (~5.0%).
xa: Ranks 5–7: **Calcium 3.6**, **Sodium 2.8**, **Potassium 2.6**.
⚠ For the whole Earth, **magnesium (13.9%)** ranks fourth after iron, oxygen and silicon.

3.s:
Consider the following statements about the composition of the Earth as a whole by mass:
1. Iron is the most abundant element.
2. Oxygen is more abundant than silicon.
3. Magnesium is more abundant than silicon.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
3.x: For the whole Earth the order is iron 32.1% > oxygen 30.1% > silicon 15.1% > magnesium 13.9%, so statement 3 is wrong.

3.s: In Suess's classification, what is the granitic continental layer of silicon and aluminium called?
3.x: SIAL (silicon-aluminium) is granitic and continental; SIMA is basaltic and NIFE the nickel-iron core.
xa: These are **Suess's chemical layers** of the Earth.
The crust's most abundant element is **oxygen (46.6%)**; the whole Earth's is **iron (32.1%)**.

3.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
3.x: Aluminium (8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust; iron (5.0%) is second. Iron leads only for the whole Earth.

3.s: Which is the second-most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
3.x: Iron, at 5.0% by weight, is the second-most abundant metal after aluminium (8.1%).

3.s: In Suess's classification, what does NIFE refer to?
3.x: NIFE is the nickel-iron core; SIAL is the granitic continental layer and SIMA the basaltic layer.

3.s: "Rama Setu" or "Adam's Bridge" is a chain of?
3.src: APPSC ASO Mains General Studies & Mental Ability 2017
3.x: Adam's Bridge (Rama Setu) is a chain of limestone shoals between Pamban Island and Mannar.

3.s: Basalt is an
3.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer General S
3.x: Basalt forms when lava cools fast on the surface – a fine-grained extrusive igneous rock.

3.s: Petrology is
3.src: APPSC Group-II Paper-I General Studies & Mental Ability 2019
3.x: Petrology is the study (science) of rocks, a part of geology.

3.s: Which of the following Rock is not a Igneous rock?
3.x: Quartzite is metamorphic (from sandstone); granite, basalt and pegmatite are igneous.

3.s: The rocks in Himalayan Mountains are?
3.x: The Himalayas are folded sedimentary rocks of the Tethys Sea; granite is a rock, not a class, and igneous/metamorphic rocks are only in the core.

3.s: Study of soil in its natural setting is known in English as
3.x: Pedology is the study of soils in their natural setting; petrology studies rocks and geology the Earth as a whole.

3.s: These rocks were used in the construction of Red Fort and Agra Fort in India.
3.x: The Red Fort and Agra Fort are built of red sandstone, a sedimentary rock.

3.s: Coal is an example of –
3.x: Coal is an organically formed sedimentary rock.

3.s: What is Marble?
3.x: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed from limestone under heat and pressure.

3.s: Origin of Metamorphic rocks occurs from …….. rock ?
3.x: Metamorphic rocks form from both igneous and sedimentary rocks under heat and pressure.

3.s: Which one of the following is not associated with the 'group'?
3.x: Gneiss is metamorphic; sandstone, limestone and shale are sedimentary, so gneiss is the odd one.

3.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of sedimentary rocks?
3.x: Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate are sedimentary rocks. The other groups contain igneous or metamorphic rocks.
3.tq: Classify every option by identifying the rock type of each member.
xs: **Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate** are all sedimentary — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) — **granite, basalt, gabbro, dolerite** — are all **igneous**.
Option (3) — **marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss** — are all **metamorphic**.
Option (4) mixes igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (sandstone) and metamorphic (marble).
xa: Other sedimentary rocks: **coal** and **chalk**; **coal** is sedimentary (organic).
Igneous also includes **pegmatite**; metamorphic also includes **schist**.

3.s: Carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater helps weathering by forming which of the following?
3.x: Carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which helps weather rocks.
3.tq: Test the chemical agent involved in carbon cycling and weathering.
xs: CO2 in rain forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rock — option **(1)** is correct.
The carbon ends up stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.
xa: **Enhanced rock weathering**: crushed fast-weathering **basalt** on farmland locks up CO2 as **bicarbonate**.
Glacier-crushed **pyrite** in the upper **Indus** basin releases CO2 about **three times** faster than silicate weathering removes it.

3.s: What is the branch of geology that studies rocks called?
3.x: Petrology is the study of rocks; it recognises three types – igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.

3.s: Which of the following is not a form of Calcium Carbonate?
3.src: APPSC ASO Mains General Studies & Mental Ability 2017
3.x: Granite is a silicate igneous rock; limestone, chalk and marble are all calcium carbonate.

3.s: Which of the following rocks consist of large grained crystals?
3.x: Plutonic (intrusive) rocks cool slowly at depth and so have large crystals; extrusive rocks are fine-grained and shale and loess are sedimentary.

3.s: The rocks in the Himalayan system are primarily characterised as
3.x: The Himalayas are made primarily of sedimentary rocks (folded Tethys sediments); plutonic rock and dykes occur only locally.

3.s: Granite is a/an:
3.x: Granite is coarse-grained and solidifies slowly beneath the surface – an intrusive igneous rock.

3.s: Which of the following rocks is not likely to contain fossils?
3.x: Granite, formed from magma, has no fossils; conglomerate, shale and sandstone are sedimentary and may hold fossils.

3.s: Which statement of the following is true for igneous rocks?
o: They are both crystal and non-crystal
3.x: Igneous rocks are both crystalline and non-crystalline; they have no fossils (not 'little'), are poorly porous and are made of silicates.

3.s: Which type of rock is formed from cooling and solidification of lava ?
3.x: Rocks formed by cooling and solidification of magma or lava are igneous.

3.s: Which of the following is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock?
3.x: Intrusive rocks cool slowly at depth, forming coarse grains, as in granite and gabbro.
xa: **Extrusive (volcanic)** lava cools fast at the surface → **fine-grained**: **basalt, rhyolite, andesite**.
APPSC G2 **2024**: **granite = intrusive igneous**.
**Hypabyssal** rocks occur in **dykes and sills** — e.g. **dolerite**.

3.s: Which of the following is a felsic extrusive igneous rock?
3.x: Rhyolite is felsic extrusive; granite is felsic intrusive, diorite intermediate intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.
xa: **Gabbro** is the **mafic intrusive** counterpart of basalt.
**Andesite** is another extrusive (volcanic) rock.
Volcanic rocks (**andesite, dacite, rhyolite, basalt**) need more energy to fracture than many sedimentary rocks.

3.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Felsic igneous rocks are generally light-coloured and silica-rich.
2. Mafic rocks are always less dense than felsic rocks.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
3.x: Felsic rocks are silica-rich, light-coloured and relatively low in density; mafic rocks, rich in iron, magnesium and calcium, are dark and dense, so statement 2 is wrong.
xa: ⚠ APPSC **2024** Assertion-Reason: "felsic rocks contain high iron, magnesium and calcium" is **false** — that describes **mafic** rocks.
Intrusive examples: felsic = **granite**; intermediate = **diorite**; mafic = **gabbro**.
Mafic minerals include **olivine** and **pyroxene**.

3.s: What are dark, dense igneous rocks rich in iron, magnesium and calcium called?
3.x: Mafic (basic) rocks are rich in Fe, Mg and Ca; felsic rocks are silica-rich and light-coloured.

3.s: Which type of rock is diorite?
3.x: Diorite is intermediate intrusive; rhyolite is felsic extrusive, granite felsic intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.

3.s: The Lakshadweep archipelago is formed on?
3.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2017
3.x: Lakshadweep is a group of coral atolls; it is not built on andesite, igneous or metamorphic rock. Moved to the Indian islands row.

3.s:
Consider the following statements made about the sedimentary rocks:
1. Sedimentary rocks are formed at Earth's surface by the hydrological system.
2. The formation of sedimentary rocks involves the weathering of pre-existing rocks.
3. Sedimentary rocks contain fossils.
4. Sedimentary rocks typically occur in layers. Which of these statements are correct?
3.x: All four are correct: sedimentary rocks form at the surface through the hydrological system, from weathering of older rocks, contain fossils and occur in layers.

3.s:
Consider the following statements:
1.
Statement I: In the context of effect of water on rocks, chalk is known as a very permeable rock whereas clay is known as quite an impermeable or least permeable rock.
2. Statement II: Chalk is porous and hence can absorb water.
3. Statement III: Clay is not at all porous. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? Physical Geography PMF IAS Geo – 2
o: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement III are correct but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct
3.x: Chalk is porous and so absorbs water (II correct, explains I); clay is porous but impermeable, so III ('not at all porous') is wrong.

3.s: Regarding sedimentary rocks which of the following statements is true?
o: These are such rocks whose structure depend on
These rocks are deposited in layers
These rocks cannot be formed in water
3.x: Sedimentary rocks are deposited in layers (strata); they are not crystalline and most form in water.

3.s: Sandstone is flaky rock, because –
o: It is formed in the desert
It is formed due to Heat
It is formed on the mountain
3.x: Sandstone is a layered (flaky) rock because its sand grains were deposited under water.

3.s: Sedimentary rocks are called ‘stratified rocks’ because they are generally formed as:
o: Successive layers of deposited, compacted and cemented sediments
Single layers of volcanic ash only
Metamorphosed rocks melted beneath the crust
3.x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
3.tq: Connect the descriptive term with its formation process.
xs: Sedimentary rocks form as **successive layers** of **deposited, compacted and cemented** sediments — option **(1)** is correct.
These layers are called **strata**, hence **"stratified rocks"**.
Unlayered crystallised magma (option 4) describes **igneous** rock.
xa: The hardening of sediments is called **lithification**.
Sedimentary rocks **may contain fossils** and host **coal, petroleum, natural gas**.

3.s: Which of the following pairs (mode of formation – sedimentary rock) is correctly matched?
3.x: Rock salt is chemically formed; sandstone is mechanically formed and coal organically formed.
xa: Other chemical examples: **halite, chert**.
Other organic examples: **chalk**, coral limestone, **geyserite**.
⚠ Coal is **sedimentary (organic)** — a common odd-one-out trap.

3.s: Which of the following describes clay with respect to porosity and permeability?
3.x: Clay has pore spaces, but its very fine particles prevent easy passage of water, so it is porous but impermeable.
xa: **Chalk and sandstone** are both porous and permeable.
**Granite** is neither porous nor permeable.
**Shale / clay** metamorphoses into **slate**.

3.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about rocks?

Granite is extrusive igneous and basalt is intrusive igneous
Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks altered by heat or pressure
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition
3.x: It is the reverse: granite is intrusive igneous and basalt is extrusive igneous.
n: Igneous rocks form through cooling or solidification of magma or lava. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock is altered by heat or pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Granite is an intrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]

3.x: Gneiss usually forms from granite; limestone gives marble, sandstone quartzite and shale slate.

3.x: Shale (clay rock) changes into slate under heat and pressure; slate can further become schist.

3.x: Markapur in Prakasam district has slate quarries; slate is a metamorphic rock formed from shale.

3.x: Metamorphism of basalt gives amphibolite and schist.

3.s: What is quartz, a major component of granite and sandstone, chemically?
3.x: Quartz is silicon dioxide (SiO2), hard and resistant to weathering, and a major component of granite and sandstone.
xa: Quartz is a **tectosilicate** (framework), like **albite** and **orthoclase**.

3.s: Feldspar makes up approximately what proportion of the Earth's crust?

xa: **Olivine** is a **nesosilicate** (isolated tetrahedra).
Tectosilicates (framework) include **albite, orthoclase** and **quartz**.

3.s: Which of the following pairs (mineral – position in Bowen's reaction series) is correctly matched?
o: Quartz – Crystallises last and is most stable
3.x: Quartz crystallises last from cooling magma and is the most stable mineral in Bowen's reaction series; olivine crystallises first.

3.s: In the discontinuous branch of Bowen's reaction series, which is the first mineral to crystallise?
3.x: The discontinuous branch runs olivine → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite; mafic minerals form first at the highest temperature.
xa: The series ends with **K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz**; **quartz is last** and most stable.
Bowen's series shows the order of **crystallisation from cooling magma** (APPSC **2024**).

3.s: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 7?

xs: **Quartz** has a Mohs hardness of **7** — option **(4)** is correct.
On the scale, **apatite** is 5, **orthoclase** 6 and **topaz** 8.
xa: The scale runs **1–10**: from **talc** (1) to **diamond (10)**; **corundum** sits just below diamond.
Quartz (**SiO2**) forms a major part of **granite and sandstone** and crystallises **last** in Bowen's series.

3.x: Hornblende (amphibole) is a double-chain inosilicate; augite is single chain and mica a phyllosilicate.

3.x: On the Mohs scale topaz is 8; apatite is 5, orthoclase 6 and calcite 3.

3.s: What are the important agents of metamorphism?
3.x: Heat and pressure transform igneous and sedimentary rocks; complete melting is not required and would lead to magma.
xa: **Melting** in the rock cycle produces **magma**, which forms **igneous** rock.
Examples: **limestone → marble**, **sandstone → quartzite**, **granite → gneiss**.

xa: Rain CO2 forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rock; carbon is stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.

3.s: In the rock cycle, through which process do deposited sediments become sedimentary rock?
3.x: After weathering, erosion and deposition, lithification forms sedimentary rocks; heat and pressure then form metamorphic rocks and melting forms magma.
xa: Full cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.
**Key rule:** any rock type can turn into any other.
Sedimentary rock forms through **burial, compaction, cementation**.

3.s: In the rock cycle, what can exposed metamorphic rocks weather into?
3.x: Exposed metamorphic rocks can weather into sediment; any rock type can be transformed into another.
xa: Mantle link: rock material comes up in **eruptions**; **subducted crust** melts back into the mantle.
Cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.

xa: ⚠ Some notes print the year as **1782** — the correct year is **1872**.
**Archaean** rocks: older than **2,500 million years**; granites, gneisses, schists; **no fossils**.

3.s: The plateau region in the south western portion of Andhra Pradesh part of the Deccan (peninsular India), and commonly called Rayalaseema, is composed of the ___ rock.
3.x: The Rayalaseema plateau, part of the Deccan, is made of Archaean gneissic (granite-gneiss) rocks; schist, shale and gabbro are not its main rock.

3.s: Which is the oldest basin in Andhra Pradesh?
3.x: The Kadapa (Cuddapah) Basin, a Proterozoic basin, is the oldest basin of AP; Nagarjuna hill and Sanganakallu are sites, not basins.

3.s: In which of the following rock systems of Andhra Pradesh can oil and petroleum be found?
3.x:
Official key: Pleistocene. Strictly, the KG basin oil and gas lie in Cretaceous–Tertiary marine sediments beneath the Pleistocene coastal cover (general knowledge, not checked).
The key is the Pleistocene system: NextGen extends it along all coastal districts, where the KG basin oil and gas occur. Dharwar, Archaean and Cuddapah rocks hold no petroleum.

3.s: A huge amount of sources found in the Vindhya rocks are of –
3.x: The Vindhyan sedimentary rocks are rich in limestone (with sandstone, china clay) – base of the cement industry. Moved to the Indian rock systems row.

3.s: With which formation are the khondalites and charnockites of Andhra Pradesh associated?
3.x: They are Archaean rocks, over 2.5 billion years old, associated with the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt.
xa: Khondalite is **not Vindhyan** (PYQ).
The Eastern Ghats belt holds **bauxite (Araku), manganese, graphite**.

3.s: At which place is gold mining reviving in Andhra Pradesh's Dharwar greenstone belt?
3.x: Gold mining is reviving at Ramagiri (July 2026), the gold belt of Andhra Pradesh's Dharwar formation.

3.s:
Consider the following statements about the Deccan Trap patches of Andhra Pradesh:
1. They consist of basalt.
2. They are associated with black cotton soil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
3.x: The Deccan Trap patches are basalt, and weathering of that basalt gives black cotton soil, so both are correct.

3.s: The Ramagiri gold belt of Andhra Pradesh is associated with which formation?
3.x: The Dharwar formation (schists and gneisses) occurs in Anantapuramu, Chittoor and YSR Kadapa and includes the Ramagiri gold belt.
xa: Gold mining is **reviving at Ramagiri** (Dharwar **greenstone belt**) (Jul **2026**).
⚠ **Mangampeta** = barytes; **Araku** = bauxite; **Ramagiri** = gold.

3.s: The Kurnool group is distinguished from the Cuddapah basin because it is associated with:
o: Cement-grade limestone and no metallic minerals
Gold and manganese in a greenstone belt
Bauxite and graphite in the Eastern Ghats
3.x: The Kurnool group contains cement-grade limestone, has no metallic minerals, and has petroleum potential.
3.tq: Compare neighbouring geological units by their distinctive resource combinations.
xs: The **Kurnool group** has **cement-grade limestone** and **no metallic minerals** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Coal** = **Gondwana**; **gold/manganese greenstone belt** = **Dharwar**; **bauxite, graphite** = **Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt**.
xa: Kurnool group: **Kurnool, Nandyal**; rocks **limestone, sandstone, shale**; also **petroleum potential**.
Kadapa–Kurnool limestone makes **Rayalaseema** a **cement hub**.

3.s: The Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt in Andhra Pradesh is associated with which one of the following resource combinations?
o: Copper, gold and cement-grade limestone only
3.x: The Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt contains bauxite, including at Araku, along with manganese and graphite.
3.tq: Use a resource-combination question to separate the Eastern Ghats from the Cuddapah and KG basins.
xs: The **Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt** holds **bauxite, manganese, graphite** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Cement-grade limestone** = **Kurnool group**; **oil and gas** = **KG basin**; **barytes, asbestos, cobalt** = **Cuddapah basin**.
xa: Rocks: **khondalite, charnockite**, quartzite, gneiss; districts **Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, ASR**.
⚠ **Araku** = bauxite.
Mining must respect **tribal areas and biodiversity**.

3.s: Which of the following pairs (place in Andhra Pradesh – mineral) is correctly matched?
3.x: Ramagiri is the gold belt; Mangampeta is known for barytes and Araku for bauxite.

3.s: Which is the largest sedimentary basin of Andhra Pradesh?
3.x: The Cuddapah basin (YSR Kadapa, Nandyal, Kurnool) is the largest sedimentary basin of Andhra Pradesh.

3.s: Which one of the following is NOT associated with the Cuddapah basin?
3.x: The Cuddapah basin contains barytes, limestone, asbestos, copper, nickel and cobalt. Coal is associated with the Gondwana formation.
3.tq: Find the resource belonging to another formation rather than the basin named in the question.
xs: **Coal** is NOT a Cuddapah basin resource — option **(4)** is correct; coal is **Gondwana** (East Godavari, ASR).
The Cuddapah basin has **barytes (Mangampeta)**, **limestone**, asbestos, copper, nickel, **cobalt**.
xa: ⚠ **Mangampeta** = barytes (Cuddapah basin).
Kadapa–Kurnool limestone makes **Rayalaseema** a **cement hub**.

3.s: In which basin of Andhra Pradesh are oil and natural gas found?
3.x: The KG basin, with marine sediments in Krishna, Eluru, Kakinada and Konaseema districts, holds AP's oil and natural gas.

3.s: Mangampeta in the Cuddapah basin of Andhra Pradesh is known for which mineral?
3.x: Mangampeta holds barytes; Araku has bauxite and Ramagiri has gold.

3.s: Over which districts of Andhra Pradesh does the Cuddapah basin mainly spread?
o: East Godavari and Alluri Sitharama Raju
3.x: The Cuddapah basin, the largest sedimentary basin of AP, spreads over YSR Kadapa, Nandyal and Kurnool districts.

3.s: In which districts of Andhra Pradesh are Gondwana coal deposits found?
o: East Godavari and Alluri Sitharama Raju
3.x: The Gondwana formation of AP, which holds coal, lies in East Godavari and Alluri Sitharama Raju districts.

3.s: In which districts of Andhra Pradesh are the Deccan Trap patches found?
3.x: Deccan Trap basalt patches in AP lie in Prakasam, Palnadu and Guntur and weather into black cotton soil.

3.s: Read the following statements and choose the correct option : Statement - I : J.D. Dana prepared a special Geological Time Scale to indicate the geological history of Indian subcontinent rocks Statement - II : As per Geological Time Scale, Indian rocks are subdivided into Archaean, Puranic, Dravidian and Aryan periods
o: Statement - I and Statement - II both are true
Statement -I and Statement - II both are false
Statement - I is true but Statement - II is false
Statement - I is false but Statement - II is true
3.x: Statement I is false – Sir T.H. Holland (GSI), not J.D. Dana, made the Indian scale; Statement II is true (Archaean, Purana, Dravidian, Aryan). Moved to the Indian rock systems row.

4.s: News reporters attached with security forces are called
4.src: APPSC Assistant Telugu Translator General Studies & Mental A
4.x: Reporters attached to and travelling with military/security units are 'embedded' reporters.

4.s: Which of the following features is NOT common in Chordates and non-chordates?
4.src: APPSC General Studies & Mental Ability (Common Paper: Hostel
4.x: Printed key: bilateral symmetry – all chordates are bilaterally symmetrical, but many non-chordates (cnidarians, adult echinoderms) are radial, so it is not common to both groups. Off-topic (zoology), moved.

4.s:
Consider the following statements:

A. The Earth's magnetic field has reversed every few hundred thousand years.

B. When the Earth was created more than 4000 million years ago, there was 54% Oxygen and no Carbon dioxide.

C. When living organisms originated, they modified the early atmosphere of the Earth.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
4.x: The magnetic field has reversed many times (A true); the early atmosphere had no free oxygen, not 54% (B false); life (photosynthesis) changed the atmosphere (C true) → A and C only.

4.s: The theory that states "pieces of the Earth's crust are in constant, slow motion driven by movement in the mantle" is called:
4.x: 'Pieces of the crust in constant slow motion driven by the mantle' is the theory of plate tectonics.

4.s: On the earth, originally, there was only one huge landmass which is known as –
4.x: The single original landmass was Pangaea; Panthalassa was the ocean, Laurasia and Gondwanaland its later halves.

4.s: Based on following statements choose the correct option: Statement - I : Theory of Plate tectonics was given by H.H. Hess in 1967. Statement - II : Theory of Plate Tectonics is based on Theory of Seafloor Spreading.
o: Statement - I and Statement - II both are true
Statement - I and Statement- II both are false
Statement - I is true but Statement - II is false
Statement - I is false but Statement - II is true
4.x: Plate tectonics was put together in 1967 by McKenzie, Parker and Morgan (Hess gave sea-floor spreading), so I is false; it is based on sea-floor spreading, so II is true.

4.s: The theory of continental drift was developed by-
4.x: Continental drift was put forward by Alfred Wegener (1912); Hess gave sea-floor spreading and Wilson/Du Toit came later.

4.s: Based on following statements choose the correct option: Statement - I : Theory of Plate tectonics was given by H.H. Hess in 1967 Statement - II : Theory of Plate Tectonics is based on Theory of Sea floor Spreading
o: Statement - I and Statement - II both are true
Statement - I and Statement- II both are false
Statement - I is true but Statement - II is false
Statement - I is false but Statement - II is true
4.x: Statement I is false (plate tectonics: McKenzie, Parker, Morgan 1967; Hess gave sea-floor spreading); Statement II is true.

4.s: With which of the following was Wegener's 'pole-fleeing force' associated?
o: The gravity of the Sun and the Moon
4.x: The pole-fleeing force was linked to Earth's rotation and the tidal force to the Sun and Moon; both were too weak, so the theory was not accepted.
xa: **Arthur Holmes** (**1930s**) gave drift the driving force Wegener lacked — **convection currents**.
Wegener proposed continental drift in **1912**.

4.s: Who proposed the convection current theory as an explanation for the movement of crustal plates?
4.x: Arthur Holmes proposed the convection current theory in the 1930s.
4.tq: Distinguish the proponent of the driving mechanism from proponents of continental drift and sea-floor spreading.
xs: **Arthur Holmes** proposed the **convection current theory** (**1930s**) — option **(4)** is correct.
**Wegener** gave continental drift (**1912**); **Harry Hess** sea-floor spreading (**1961**); **Vine** (with Matthews) explained magnetic stripes (**1963**).
xa: **Radioactive decay heat** in the mantle drives the convection currents.
Plate tectonics' driving force is **mantle convection** (Arthur Holmes).

4.s: In Holmes's convection-current theory, what is the source of the heat that drives mantle convection?
4.x: Radioactive heat drives convection; rising limbs split crust at ridges and sinking limbs drag plates at trenches.
xa: Holmes gave drift the **driving force Wegener lacked**.
**Hess (1961)**: magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges**; crust is destroyed at **trenches**.

4.s: Who proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s?
4.x: Harry Hess proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s, including the creation of new crust at mid-ocean ridges and its destruction at trenches.
4.tq: Use direct person–theory identification and distinguish the proponent from related plate-tectonic thinkers.
xs: **Harry Hess** proposed **sea-floor spreading** in **1961** (early 1960s) — option **(4)** is correct.
**Wegener** = continental drift (**1912**); **Arthur Holmes** = convection currents (**1930s**).
xa: Magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges**, new crust spreads sideways and is destroyed at **trenches**.
**Vine and Matthews (1963)** explained the **symmetrical magnetic bands** supporting it.

4.s: How do normal and reversed magnetic polarity bands occur on either side of a mid-ocean ridge?
4.x: Ridge rocks preserve the field of their time, giving alternating normal and reversed bands symmetrically on both sides.
xa: The bands were explained by **Vine and Matthews, 1963**.
**Brunhes–Matuyama** reversal: **780,000** years ago.

4.s: The theory of plate tectonics was put together in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker and independently by whom?
4.x: McKenzie and Parker developed the theory in 1967, and Morgan proposed it independently.
4.tq: Pair the principal proponents with the correct year and contribution.
xs: Plate tectonics was put together in **1967** by **McKenzie and Parker**, and independently by **Morgan** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Wegener** = drift (**1912**); **Holmes** = convection (**1930s**); **Bullard** = jig-saw computer fit (**1964**).
xa: The lithosphere is broken into **rigid plates** floating on the semi-fluid **asthenosphere**.
Driving force: **mantle convection**.

4.s: On which layer do the lithospheric plates float?
4.x: The rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that float on the semi-fluid asthenosphere.
4.tq: Distinguish the rigid layer from the underlying semi-fluid layer.
xs: Lithospheric plates float on the **semi-fluid asthenosphere** — option **(2)** is correct.
The lithosphere is broken into **rigid plates**.
xa: Plate tectonics: **1967**, **McKenzie and Parker**, independently **Morgan**.
There are **seven major plates** (APPSC **2018**).

4.s: Why was Wegener's continental drift theory rejected?
o: It was based on GPS data
His proposed forces were too weak
It denied the existence of Pangaea
4.x: Wegener's pole-fleeing and tidal forces were too weak to move continents; Holmes later supplied the driving force.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: Who explained in 1963 the symmetrical normal and reversed magnetic bands on either side of a ridge?
4.x: Vine and Matthews (1963) explained the palaeomagnetic stripes; McKenzie and Parker put plate tectonics together in 1967.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: In which year did Alfred Wegener put forward the theory of continental drift?
4.x: Wegener gave continental drift in 1912; Holmes (1930s), Hess (1961) and plate tectonics (1967) came later.

4.s: The chief contributor to Global warming in the present and last century is?
4.src: Previous paper (title page not in scan)
4.x: Warming of the last and present century is driven mainly by human (anthropogenic) greenhouse-gas emissions (IPCC AR6), not tectonics, volcanoes or Earth's rotation.

4.s: Which American Gymnast created history as first American women gymnast to win most gold medals in single Olympics?
4.src: APPSC AE (Subordinate Services) Mains General Studies & Ment
4.x: Simone Biles won four golds at Rio 2016, the most by an American woman gymnast at a single Games.

4.s: Which of the following was discovered by Columbus?
4.src: APPSC Junior Assistant cum Typist in Prisons & Correctional
4.x: Columbus (1492) reached the Americas while seeking a western route to India; India's sea route was found by Vasco da Gama in 1498. Moved to history.

4.s: The largest ozone hole is observed over
4.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
4.x: The largest (seasonal) ozone hole lies over Antarctica, not over Africa, Australia or India. Moved to the atmosphere row.

4.s: Which of the following continents witnessed total solar eclipse in August, 2017?
4.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II (Male & Female) in AP
4.x: The total solar eclipse of 21 August 2017 crossed the USA coast to coast, i.e. North America. Moved to the solar-system row.

4.s: Sierra Nevada is the name of
4.src: APPSC Group-I Paper-I Screening Test General Studies & Menta
4.x: The Sierra Nevada is a mountain range – in California (USA); a range of the same name is in Spain.

4.s: Which of the following continents was not Part of "Gondwana land"?
4.src: Assistant Director in AP Economics and Statistics 2017
4.x: Europe was part of Laurasia, the northern landmass; Gondwana included Peninsular India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica.

4.s: Which continent has the largest number of people living in poverty
4.src: Dental Assistant Surgeons, Zilla Sainik Welfare Officer, Ass
4.x: Africa (Sub-Saharan) now has the largest number of people in extreme poverty – about 7 in 10 of the world's extreme poor in 2023; Asia's share has fallen sharply.

4.s: India was the part of ancient Gondwana land Supercontinent. It includes the following landmass of the present :
4.x: Gondwanaland included South America, Africa, Australia (with Antarctica, Madagascar, Arabia, India) – all of the above.

4.s: The southern continent broken from Pangaea is called:
o: More than one of the above
4.x: The southern continent broken from Pangaea is Gondwanaland; Laurasia is the northern one.

4.s: The Indian subcontinent was originally part of a huge land mass called
4.x: Peninsular India was part of the southern supercontinent Gondwana.

4.s: Which one of the following continents was not a part of Gondwana Land?
4.x: North America belonged to Laurasia, not Gondwanaland; South America, Africa and Australia were Gondwana.

4.s: What was the name of the mega-ocean that surrounded Pangaea?
4.x: Panthalassa surrounded Pangaea; the Tethys Sea lay between northern Laurasia and southern Gondwanaland.
xa: Laurasia: **North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia (minus India)**.
Gondwanaland: **South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar, Arabia**.

4.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of landmasses assigned to Gondwanaland?
o: South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica
North America, Greenland, Europe and Asia
Europe, India, North America and Greenland
Asia, Africa, Europe and South America
4.x: Gondwanaland included South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar and Arabia.
4.tq: Classify a group by checking every member against the southern supercontinent.
xs: **South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica** were all part of **Gondwanaland** — option **(1)** is correct.
**North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia** formed **Laurasia** (options 2–4 mix in Laurasian lands).
xa: Gondwanaland also included **Madagascar** and **Arabia**.
⚠ India = **Gondwanaland**, not Laurasia (APPSC **2018**: India is part of **Gondwana Land**).

4.s: Which landmasses did the Tethys Sea separate?
4.x: Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, separated by the Tethys Sea.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: Which of the following was a part of Laurasia?
4.x: Laurasia included North America, Greenland, Europe and Asia minus India; India, Australia and Madagascar were Gondwanaland.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: Gandhiji suggested two fold strategies to resolve community problems. Select the correct option
4.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer General S
4.x: Gandhi's two-fold method for resolving conflicts was non-violence (ahimsa) and satyagraha (truth-force).

4.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. According to Continental Drift Theory, about 150 million years ago, Pangaea, the super continent, had split into Laurasia and Gondwanaland.

II. About 65 million years ago, Godwanaland further broke up to give rise to other continents.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
4.src: APPSC Group-II Screening Test (General Studies & Mental Abil
4.x: No key: NCERT puts Pangaea's split into Laurasia and Gondwanaland at about 200 million years ago (not 150), while some textbooks use 150 and 65 million years; the official APPSC key could not be found, so neither 'I only', 'II only', 'both' nor 'none' can be confirmed.

4.s:
Which of the following are the evidence of the phenomenon of continental drift?
I. The belt of ancient rocks from Brazil coast matches with those from Western Africa.
II. The gold deposits of Ghana are derived from the Brazil plateau when the two continents lay side by side.
III. The Gondwana system of sediments from India is known to have its counterparts in six different landmasses of the Southern Hemisphere.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
4.x: All three are NCERT evidence: the Brazil–West Africa rock belts, Ghana's gold derived from the Brazil plateau, and the Gondwana sediments with counterparts in six southern landmasses.

4.s:
Assertion (A) : Rich placer deposits of gold are found on the Ghana coast and gold-bearing veins are found in Brazil.
Reason (R) : At some point of time, these continents were joined together along the Atlantic coast.
Select the correct answer.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
4.x: Both are true and R explains A: Ghana's placer gold has no local source because its source veins are in Brazil, from which it was derived when the continents were joined.

4.s: Gondwana-type tillites in India and their counterparts in southern continents support continental drift. What do tillites indicate?
4.x: Tillites are glacial deposits. Their distribution across India and other southern continents indicates that these areas were formerly connected and experienced common glacial conditions.
4.tq: Identify the process represented by a geological deposit.
xs: **Tillites** are **glacial deposits**, so they indicate **ancient glacial conditions** — option **(1)** is correct.
India's **Gondwana-type tillites** have counterparts in the **other southern continents**, showing they were once joined.
xa: Other evidences: **jig-saw fit**, **same-age rocks**, **placer deposits**, **fossils** (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris).
India belonged to **Gondwanaland**, not Laurasia.

4.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Placer deposits — Ghana and Brazil source region
Same-age rocks — Brazil and Western Africa
Jigsaw fit — South America and Africa coastlines
4.x: Mesosaurus is associated with South Africa and Brazil. The other three pairs correctly represent evidence for continental drift.
4.tq: Find the incorrectly paired evidence and geographical occurrence.
xs: **Mesosaurus — India and Australia only** is wrongly matched — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mesosaurus** is found in **South Africa and Brazil**.
The other pairs are right: **placer gold** (Ghana, source in Brazil), **same-age rocks** (Brazil–Western Africa), **jig-saw fit** (South America–Africa).
xa: **Lemurs** in **India, Madagascar, Africa** gave rise to the idea of "**Lemuria**".
**Glossopteris** flora is another fossil evidence.

4.s: The ancient rock belts of about 2,000 million years on the Brazil coast match belts found in which region?
4.x: Ancient rock belts on the Brazil coast match rock belts of the same age in Western Africa.
4.tq: Connect the numerical age with the correct matching region.
xs: The **2,000-million-year** rock belts of the **Brazil coast** match those of **Western Africa** — option **(1)** is correct.
This is the "**rocks of the same age** across oceans" evidence (UPSC **2025**).
xa: **Placer gold** of the **Ghana coast** has its source in the **Brazil plateau** (UPSC **2025**).
UPSC **2025** counted rock belts, placer gold and a third evidence as **all correct**.
**Bullard's 1964** computer fit matched South America and Africa.

4.s: Who is associated with the 1964 computer fit of South America and Africa?
4.x: Bullard's 1964 computer fit supported the jig-saw fit, best at the continental-shelf edge.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: Where are Mesosaurus fossils, an evidence of continental drift, found?
4.x: Mesosaurus occurs in South Africa and Brazil, not in India and Australia.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: Which fossil flora is cited as an evidence of continental drift?
4.x: Glossopteris fossils occur in India and the other southern continents, showing they were once joined in Gondwanaland.

4.s: The age, density, and thickness of oceanic crust ____ with distance from the mid-ocean ridge.
4.src: APPSC Assistant Director of Economics, Assistant Commissione
4.x: Away from the mid-ocean ridge the age, density and thickness of oceanic crust (and sediment) increase.

4.s: The process that continually adds new crust is:
4.x: Sea-floor spreading at mid-ocean ridges continually adds new crust; subduction destroys it.

4.s: The direct observation of sea-floor spreading in bursts was associated with which conclusion?
o: Sea-floor spreading occurs only at continental interiors.
Sea-floor spreading may take place in episodic bursts.
Sea-floor spreading always occurs at a constant rate.
Sea-floor spreading is unrelated to lava outpouring.
4.x: The observed rapid episode of sinking, spreading and lava emplacement suggested that sea-floor spreading can occur in bursts rather than at a uniform rate.
4.tq: Infer the process characteristic from the observed event rather than from a general definition.
xs: The first direct in-situ observation showed **sea-floor spreading happens in bursts** — option **(2)** is correct.
The seafloor sank **4 m**, spread over **1 m**, with **160 million cubic metres** of lava in **16 days**.
xa: **Harry Hess (1961)**: magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges** and new crust spreads sideways.
Crust age, density and thickness **increase with distance from the ridge** (APPSC **2019**).

4.s: Moving away from a mid-ocean ridge, which one of the following trends is observed in oceanic crust and its sediment cover?
o: Age increases, while density and thickness decrease.
Only sediment thickness increases; crustal age and density remain unchanged.
Age, density and thickness decrease continuously.
4.x: The age, density and thickness of oceanic crust, along with the thickness of its sediment cover, increase with distance from the ridge.
4.tq: Apply the directional trend rule by comparing conditions near the ridge with those farther away.
xs: Away from the ridge, **age, density and thickness increase** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC **2019**).
The **sediment cover** also thickens with distance from the ridge.
xa: Ocean-floor rocks are **far younger** than continental rocks; the oldest are ~**200 million years**.
New crust forms at the **ridge** and is destroyed at **trenches**.

4.s: The oldest rocks of the ocean floor are approximately how old?
4.x: Ocean-floor rocks are much younger than continental rocks; the oldest are about 200 million years old.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: How many plates does the 'theory of Plate Tectonics' consist of?
4.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020
4.x: Plate tectonics recognises seven major plates (Pacific, N. American, S. American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic).

4.s: Cocos Plate lies between-
4.x: The Cocos Plate lies between Central America and the Pacific Plate; Nazca lies off South America.

4.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the seven major plates listed in plate tectonics?
4.x: The seven listed major plates are Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic. Nazca is a minor plate.
4.tq: Separate a minor plate from the standard list of major plates.
xs: The **Nazca** plate is a **minor** plate, not one of the seven major — option **(1)** is correct.
The **7 major plates**: **Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic**.
xa: Minor plates: **Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji**.
Nazca lies between **South America** and the **Pacific plate**.

4.s: Between which plates does the Nazca Plate lie?
4.x: The Nazca Plate is located between the South American Plate and the Pacific Plate.
4.tq: Test a minor plate by its bordering major plates.
xs: The **Nazca** plate lies between **South America** and the **Pacific plate** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Caroline** = between the Philippine and Indian plates; **Philippine** = between the Asiatic and Pacific plates; **Owen Fracture** separates African and Indian plates.
xa: ⚠ **Cocos** = Central America; **Nazca** = South America.
In the **Andes**, the **Nazca** plate subducts under the **South American** plate.

4.s: Which instrument-based method is used to monitor plate movement?
4.x: Plate movement is monitored using GPS data.
4.tq: Distinguish the modern monitoring technology from unrelated instruments.
xs: Plate movement is monitored using **GPS data** — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC **2021**).
Tide gauges, barometers and rain gauges measure sea level, pressure and rain — not plate motion.
xa: **GSI** runs **34 GNSS stations** tracking crustal movement and building strain models.
India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.

4.s: Between which plates does the Caroline Plate lie?
4.x: The Caroline Plate lies between the Philippine and Indian plates, north of New Guinea.
4.tq: one-liner

4.s: How many major lithospheric plates are there?
4.x: There are seven major plates: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic.

4.s: Between which plates does the Philippine Plate lie?

4.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about convergent plate boundaries?
o: New crust is added at them
Friction associated with subduction can produce earthquakes
4.x: New crust is added at divergent boundaries; convergent boundaries are destructive, with subduction friction producing earthquakes.

4.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
4.x: The San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary, not a divergent one.
xa: **Mariana Trench** = **ocean–ocean** subduction.
**Red Sea / East African Rift** = divergent (**Afar triple junction**).

4.s: How was the Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed?
o: northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys Plate
southward subduction of the Indian Plate beneath the Arabian Plate
transform motion along the San Andreas Fault
divergence between the Nubian and Somalian plates
4.x: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys Plate and lies between the Indus and Shyok suture zones.
4.tq: Match the named magmatic arc with its subducting plate and direction of subduction.
xs: The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** formed by **northward subduction** of the **Neo-Tethys** plate — option **(1)** is correct.
It lies between the **Indus and Shyok suture zones**.
xa: Its **130-million-year** history laid the base for the Himalayas.
Delamination beneath **Tibet** is another new finding on the Indian plate.

4.s: The Sagaing Fault in Myanmar is a transform boundary between which plates?
4.x: The Sagaing Fault is a conservative or transform boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates.
4.tq: Match a named fault with the plates on either side.
xs: The **Sagaing Fault** (Myanmar) is a transform boundary between the **Indian and Eurasian** plates — option **(2)** is correct.
Transform boundaries are **conservative**: plates slide past horizontally.
xa: The other classic transform fault is the **San Andreas Fault**.
Transform-boundary earthquakes come from **sudden slip**.

4.s: With which of the following are the Red Sea and the East African Rift associated?
o: divergence of the Nubian, Somalian and Arabian plates
collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
horizontal sliding of the Pacific and North American plates
subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate
4.x: The Red Sea and East African Rift are divergent settings associated with the separation of the Nubian, Somalian and Arabian plates near the Afar triple junction.
4.tq: Link a named regional feature with the specific plates and boundary process involved.
xs: The **Red Sea / East African Rift** mark **divergence** of the **Nubian, Somalian and Arabian** plates — option **(1)** is correct.
They meet at the **Afar triple junction**.
Indian–Eurasian **collision** = Himalayas; **Nazca subduction** = Andes.
xa: The **East African Rift** is a series of mostly **freshwater** lakes, with **Lake Malawi** at its southern end.
⚠ **Lake Victoria** is **not a rift lake** — it lies between the two branches (APPSC **2024**).

4.s: Which of the following pairs (example – plate boundary) is correctly matched?
4.x: The Mariana Trench is an ocean-ocean convergent boundary; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Red Sea are divergent and the Himalayas convergent.

4.s: The Owen Fracture Zone separates which two plates?
4.x: The Owen Fracture Zone separates the Arabian and Indian plates.

4.x: San Andreas is a transform (conservative) boundary where plates slide past horizontally, not divergent.

o: Subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate

4.x: The Red Sea and East African Rift form where the Nubian, Somalian and Arabian plates diverge near the Afar triple junction.

4.s: The North-Western Region of the Indian Sub-continent is susceptible to earthquake activity because of –
4.x: The north-west of the subcontinent lies on the convergent Indian–Eurasian plate boundary, so earthquakes come from plate tectonic activity, not volcanoes or corals.

4.s:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as-
Assertion (A) and the other as
Reason (R).
Assertion (A): The Himalayas are still rising.
Reason (R) : The Indian tectonic plate is colliding with the Eurasian plate.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct
4.x: Both true and R explains A: the Indian plate still pushes into the Eurasian plate (~5 cm/yr), so the Himalayas keep rising.

4.s: The paleomagnetic results obtained from India indicate that in the past, the Indian land mass has moved :
4.x: Palaeomagnetic results show the Indian landmass has moved northward from south of the equator.

4.s: Which of the following mainly explains the Himalayas and the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin?
o: Collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
4.x: The India-Eurasia collision explains the Himalayas, the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin and India's earthquake risk.
xa: The collision began **~4–5 crore (40–50 million) years ago**.
The Indian plate **closed the Tethys**; the Himalayas are **still rising**.

4.s: What does delamination in southern Tibet refer to in the context of the Indian Plate?
o: The melting of all continental crust at the surface of Tibet
The spreading apart of the Tibetan Plateau along a mid-ocean ridge
The peeling off and sinking of the denser lower layer of the plate into the mantle at about 100 km depth
The horizontal sliding of the entire Indian Plate along the Himalayan Frontal Fault
4.x: Delamination refers to the denser lower layer of the plate peeling away and sinking into the mantle at approximately 100 kilometres depth.
4.tq: Test the exact meaning of a specialised tectonic term through its mechanism and depth.
xs: **Delamination** = the denser lower layer **peeling off and sinking into the mantle** at ~**100 km** — option **(3)** is correct.
It was seen with **94 seismic stations** in southern Tibet (seismic imaging, **helium isotopes**).
xa: India **underthrust** Asia **45–20 million years ago**, lifting the Tibetan Plateau.
The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** lies between the **Indus and Shyok** suture zones.

4.s: About how many years ago did Gondwanaland break up?
4.x: Gondwanaland broke up approximately 225 million years ago.
4.tq: Distinguish the geological breakup date from the later Himalayan uplift date.
xs: **Gondwanaland broke up ~225 million years ago** — option **(3)** is correct.
**65 million years ago** is when the **Himalayas rose**, not the break-up.
xa: After the break-up, the **Indian craton** slid towards the **Eurasian craton**.
India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.

4.s: What was the Indian Plate doing when the Deccan Traps erupted?
o: crossing near the equator and passing over the Reunion hotspot
moving southward across the Tethys Sea
colliding with the Eurasian Plate in the Himalaya
4.x: The Deccan Traps erupted as the northward-moving Indian Plate crossed near the equator and passed over the Reunion hotspot.
4.tq: Connect a geological event with the plate’s position and hotspot passage at that time.
xs: The **Deccan Traps** erupted as India crossed **near the equator** over the **Reunion hotspot** — option **(2)** is correct.
India was moving **northward**, not southward; collision with Eurasia came later.
xa: ⚠ **Reunion hotspot** = Deccan Traps; **Owen Fracture** = African/Indian plates.
India was **far south** of the equator before the **Cretaceous**.

4.s: About when did the collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates begin?
4.x: The collision began approximately 4–5 crore years ago, equivalent to about 40–50 million years ago. Some older estimates place it at about 50–55 million years ago.
4.tq: Convert crore-based geological time into its equivalent million-year scale without changing the order of magnitude.
xs: The India–Eurasia collision began **~4–5 crore (40–50 million) years ago** — option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Older notes say **50–55 million** years.
xa: The Indian plate **subducted** under Eurasia and **closed the Tethys**.
India **underthrust** Asia **45–20 million years ago**, lifting the **Tibetan Plateau**.

4.s: At what rate is the Indian Plate moving northward?
4.x: The Indian Plate moves north at about 5 cm a year, so the young fold Himalayas are still rising.
xa: Uplift phases: **Eocene, Miocene and Pliocene**; began **~70 million years ago**.
The **Siwaliks** are the **youngest** range.

4.s: Until which period was the Peninsular Plateau of India a part of the African landmass?
4.x: The Peninsular Plateau, an old Gondwana shield, was part of the African landmass until the Cretaceous.
xa: **Gondwanaland broke up ~225 million years ago**.
AP's **Eastern Ghats** are old, eroded hills of the stable **Gondwana shield**, not young fold mountains.

4.s: At about what rate are the Himalayas still rising?
4.x: India moves north at about 5 cm a year, so the Himalayas are still rising by about 5 mm a year.

4.src: APPSC Assistant Executive Engineer (AEE) General Studies & M
4.x: Sudden movements inside the Earth cause earthquakes and volcanoes; continents, plateaus and oceans come from slow movements.

4.x: Orogenic movements act through horizontal forces and build mountains such as the Himalayas.

Consider the following statements about diastrophism:

4.x: Anai = elephant and malai = hill in Tamil, so the Anaimalai Hills are the 'Elephant Mountains'; Anaimudi (2,695 m) is their highest peak. Moved to the Peninsular Plateau row.

4.x: The Aravallis are made of the oldest (Archaean–Dharwar) rocks among the options; the Himalayas, Siwaliks and the Indo-Gangetic plain are young. Moved to the Indian rock systems row.

4.s: Kasi, Garo and Jaintia Hills are part of?
4.src: Civil Assistant Surgeon Vaidya Vidhana Parishad 2017
4.x: The Khasi, Garo and Jaintia hills are grouped with the Purvanchal (eastern hills). Strictly, the Meghalaya plateau is a detached part of the Peninsula (PMF), but of these options Purvanchal fits.

4.src: Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-I Screening Test 2017
